## Load Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

nhanes <- read_csv(
  "examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```
```{r}
dim(nhanes)
names(nhanes)
```

### BMI Summary by Income Group and Gender

```{r}
bmi_summary <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI),
    sd_bmi = sd(BMI),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bmi_summary
```
### Reusable R Function

```{r}
summarize_bmi <- function(data) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
    group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_bmi = mean(BMI),
      sd_bmi = sd(BMI),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

bmi_function_result <- summarize_bmi(nhanes)

bmi_function_result
```
```{r}
bmi_summary_rounded <- bmi_summary |>
  mutate(
    mean_bmi = round(mean_bmi, 2),
    sd_bmi = round(sd_bmi, 2)
  )

bmi_summary_rounded
```


## Parity Discussion

I compared the R and Python results using the same NHANES dataset.

Both languages loaded 105,626 rows and 18 columns. After removing missing values in BMI, IncomeGroup, and Gender, both retained 87,647 rows.

Both analyses produced 6 groups based on IncomeGroup and Gender. The group counts, mean BMI, and standard deviations matched after rounding to two decimal places.

The R function and Python helper also reproduced their original summary results.

No differences were identified in the checked results.
